title: Occasion: Calais, August 1802
short: Written on the beach at Calais in August 1802, during Wordsworth's visit to Annette Vallon and their daughter Caroline; published in 1807.
body: During the brief Peace of Amiens (1802) William and Dorothy Wordsworth crossed to Calais to meet Annette Vallon, whom Wordsworth had loved in France in 1791-92, and their daughter Caroline, born in December 1792, whom he had never seen. The aim was partly to settle matters before his marriage to Mary Hutchinson in October 1802. Dorothy's journal records evening walks by the sea during the month they spent there. The sonnet was published in Poems, in Two Volumes (1807). The Victorian editors who printed it did not know the child's identity; the Vallon affair became public only through G. M. Harper (1916) and Émile Legouis (1922).

title: Beauteous
short: A poetic, somewhat elevated form of 'beautiful', setting a solemn, devotional key.
body: 'Beauteous' was by Wordsworth's day a literary word, used in hymns and older poetry; together with 'calm and free' it makes the opening line a slow, stately pentameter of evening peace. 'Free' suggests both openness of space and freedom from care or constraint, and perhaps the freedom of peacetime travel. The comma-separated adjectives create an unhurried rhythm, and the line contains no strong verb, so that the poem opens in pure stillness before the motion of the sea is heard in line 6.

title: Evening as a nun at prayer
short: The hour is compared to a nun 'breathless with adoration': nature itself is at worship.
body: The simile casts the whole evening as a religious act. 'The holy time' recalls the canonical hours of prayer, particularly vespers at sunset, and the nun, silent and 'breathless' in adoration, embodies a stillness so intense that even breath is suspended. In a Protestant poet the Catholic figure is notable, and fitting to French Catholic surroundings. The enjambment of 'Nun / Breathless' briefly holds the breath across the line ending.

title: 'the mighty Being'
short: Either the sea itself, personified as a vast living presence, or God, heard in the sea's ceaseless sound; readers divide.
body: The 'mighty Being' whose 'eternal motion' makes 'a sound like thunder' can be read as the sea, the natural power before them, or as God, whose presence is heard through it. The capital B and the solemn 'doth' push toward the divine; the immediate context ('the Sea') suggests the ocean. Most commentators take the ambiguity as deliberate: the sea is the visible sign of the eternal. 'Thunder' in the Bible is often the voice of God (Psalm 29:3, 'the God of glory thundereth: the LORD is upon many waters'), which supports the reading that the sea's sound is a divine voice.

title: 'everlastingly' and the volta
short: The octave ends on a long, five-syllable adverb, after which the sestet turns to the child.
body: The sonnet is Petrarchan in shape (octave abbaacca, sestet defdfe in its rhyme pattern), and the octave ends with the dash and the single drawn-out word 'everlastingly', whose length imitates the endless sound of the sea. At line 9 the voice turns from the scene to the companion: 'Dear Child! dear Girl!' The movement from cosmic to intimate is the sonnet's central structure.

title: 'Dear Child! dear Girl!': Caroline
short: Wordsworth's French daughter Caroline, then nine years old, walking with him on the shore.
body: The child is Caroline Wordsworth (Anne-Caroline), daughter of Wordsworth and Annette Vallon. The doubled address, both tender and slightly formal, has been read as the speech of a father meeting a daughter he hardly knows. The poem neither names her nor explains the relation, and for a long time readers could not identify her. Some biographers find a note of self-justification in the sonnet's assurance that the girl's nature is divine even if she seems unmoved, a way of blessing a child he could not raise.

title: The unthinking child
short: If the child seems unaffected by the solemn scene, she is no less divine, for her holiness is unconscious.
body: This is a compact statement of a belief Wordsworth develops in the 'Intimations' Ode (begun 1802, the same year): the young child lives closer to God than the reflective adult, even without knowing it. The adult must consciously feel 'solemn thought'; the child simply is in communion. 'Therefore' answers an implied objection that piety requires awareness. The sonnet thus anticipates the Ode's 'best Philosopher', the child who reads the eternal deep without knowing it (stanza 8).

sources.cite: William Wordsworth, 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality' (1807), st. 8

title: Abraham's bosom
short: From Luke 16:22, where the beggar Lazarus is carried after death 'into Abraham's bosom': a state of blessed rest close to God.
body: In Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), the poor man dies and is carried by angels into Abraham's bosom, the place of comfort for the righteous. The phrase came to mean heaven or the bliss of the faithful. Wordsworth's twist is that the child lies there 'all the year', in this life and continuously, not after death: her ordinary existence is already blessed. RPO's annotation cross-refers the line to Luke 16:22.

title: The Temple's inner shrine
short: The Holy of Holies, the innermost sanctuary of the Jerusalem Temple, entered only by the high priest.
body: The 'inner shrine' alludes to the Holy of Holies, the innermost room of Solomon's Temple where the Ark of the Covenant stood (1 Kings 6:16-19; Hebrews 9:3-7). Only the high priest entered it, once a year. The child, by contrast, worships there constantly and without effort, an image of the most intimate access to God. The line parallels the previous one: Abraham's bosom (rest) and the inner shrine (worship).

title: 'God being with thee when we know it not'
short: The last line echoes Jacob's words at Bethel, 'Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not' (Genesis 28:16).
body: The closing line, in an absolute construction, may echo Genesis 28:16, where Jacob wakes from his dream of the ladder and realises God was present unnoticed. Here the unknowing is the adults' ('we know it not'): God is with the child even when the observers cannot perceive it, and perhaps when the child herself is unaware. The quiet monosyllables end the sonnet with the stillness of the opening.
